steps.title: Choose an OAuth app or a GitHub App
steps.detail: OAuth apps are the simplest path with Composio: one consent screen and coarse scopes. A GitHub App gives repo-level, fine-grained permissions and short-lived tokens, but each user must also install it on their account or organization, and Composio doesn't send that install link for you yet. Pick an OAuth app unless customers insist on read-only or per-repo access.

steps.title: Register the OAuth app under your company's organization
steps.detail: In your organization's settings, open Developer settings → OAuth apps → New OAuth App and enter the app name and homepage URL. Apps owned by an organization automatically get access to that organization's resources, so your own team won't need an approval.

steps.title: Add Composio's redirect URI
steps.detail: Under Redirect URIs, paste Composio's redirect URI and leave "Allow wildcard matching" off. GitHub accepts up to 10 redirect URIs, so you can keep a local one for testing.

steps.title: Generate a client secret and keep both values
steps.detail: After registering, generate a client secret on the app's page. Store the client ID and secret in your secrets manager; you'll give them to Composio in the next step.

steps.title: Create a GitHub auth config with your credentials
steps.detail: Create a custom OAuth2 auth config for the github toolkit with your client ID and secret. Composio pre-selects 7 scopes; keep only the ones your capability needs (see Scopes). Then pass the auth config ID when you create sessions.

copyValues.label: TypeScript

steps.title: Test it in the Composio Playground
steps.detail: Open the auth config, choose Connect Account, approve your own app on GitHub's consent screen, then run one GitHub tool against a repo in your organization.

steps.title: Ask each customer's organization owner to approve your app
steps.detail: Organizations with OAuth app access restrictions (on by default for new organizations) block your app from their private resources until an owner approves it. Members can request approval during sign-in; tell customers to expect that request.

blocker.symptom: The connection works but organization repositories are missing
blocker.cause: The customer's organization restricts OAuth apps and hasn't approved yours, so private organization data isn't available to it
blocker.fix: Have a member request approval and an organization owner approve it in the organization's OAuth app settings

steps.title: Skip GitHub Marketplace unless you'll sell through it
steps.detail: Listing isn't needed for customers to connect. Free listings only need to meet the listing requirements; paid plans also need publisher verification for your organization.

steps.title: Move existing users to your app
steps.detail: Users who connected through Composio's managed GitHub app stay on it until they reconnect. Once your auth config works, ask them to reconnect.

unknowns: How long customers' organization owners take to approve an app depends on each customer; GitHub publishes no estimate.
Hands-on effort is an estimate and untested.

evidence.label: official
evidence.claim: OAuth apps can be registered under a personal account or an organization you administer; GitHub suggests considering a GitHub App, which uses fine-grained permissions, gives users control over which repositories it can access, and uses short-lived tokens. You can enter up to 10 callback URLs, and 'Expire user access tokens' is on by default.
evidence.sourceTitle: GitHub Docs: Creating an OAuth app

evidence.label: official
evidence.claim: repo grants full read and write access to public and private repositories; public_repo limits access to public repositories; read:org is read-only organization membership; read:user reads profile data; workflow allows updating Actions workflow files; with no scope an app can read public information only.
evidence.sourceTitle: GitHub Docs: Scopes for OAuth apps

evidence.label: official
evidence.claim: With OAuth app access restrictions, members can't authorize OAuth apps for organization resources and must request owner approval; restrictions are on by default for new organizations; apps owned by the organization get access automatically; unapproved apps can't reach private organization resources through the API.
evidence.sourceTitle: GitHub Docs: About OAuth app access restrictions

evidence.label: official
evidence.claim: Publishing free plans on GitHub Marketplace only requires meeting the listing requirements; paid plans require publisher verification of the organization.
evidence.sourceTitle: GitHub Docs: About GitHub Marketplace for apps

evidence.label: official
evidence.claim: Composio supports bringing your own GitHub App via its client ID and secret, but the user must separately install the app and grant repository access; Composio doesn't provide the install link automatically yet.

evidence.label: official
evidence.claim: Composio's API lists https://backend.composio.dev/api/v1/auth-apps/add as the default OAuth redirect URI for the GitHub auth config, with default scopes repo, user, gist, notifications, project, workflow, codespace.
evidence.note: Also shown in the Composio dashboard when you create the auth config; use the dashboard value if they differ.

evidence.label: official
evidence.claim: To use your own OAuth app, create an auth config in the dashboard, add the redirect URI it shows to the provider's portal, copy the client ID and secret into Composio, and pass the auth config ID to sessions via authConfigs; unlisted toolkits keep using managed auth.

evidence.label: official
evidence.claim: Changing scopes affects new connections only; existing users keep granted scopes until they reconnect.

evidence.label: official
evidence.claim: Existing connections keep refreshing with their original auth config; full migration means re-authentication.

evidence.label: tested
evidence.claim: We registered a GitHub OAuth app on a personal account with Composio's redirect URI, created a custom Composio auth config, connected through Composio and ran a read-only GitHub tool in the Playground: it worked. GitHub's form now calls the field "Redirect URIs" (up to 10, with an optional "Allow wildcard matching") and has "Expire user access tokens" on by default; GitHub issued an expiring token with a refresh token, which Composio stored. Composio's form starts with 7 scopes (repo, user, gist, notifications, project, workflow, codespace); after trimming to repo and user, GitHub granted exactly those.
evidence.sourceTitle: Our test: GitHub OAuth app connected through Composio (2026-10-23)
